quiz_item.question: Why do severe wildfires frequently lead to destructive flash floods and mudslides when rain falls months after the fire is out?
options: A. Chemical fire retardants turn clay soils into impermeable concrete crusts
B. Surviving trees release excess groundwater through their damaged bark
C. Intense heat destroys root systems and creates hydrophobic soil layers that repel water
D. Ash deposits freeze the upper soil horizon and block snowmelt infiltration
choices: A. Chemical fire retardants turn clay soils into impermeable concrete crusts
B. Surviving trees release excess groundwater through their damaged bark
C. Intense heat destroys root systems and creates hydrophobic soil layers that repel water
D. Ash deposits freeze the upper soil horizon and block snowmelt infiltration
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Intense heat destroys root systems and creates hydrophobic soil layers that repel water
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): High-severity fires vaporize organic compounds that condense into a waxy, water-repellent soil layer while removing the plants and roots that normally absorb rainfall (p. 6).

D. It drives away all songbirds that would otherwise consume fallen pine needles

quiz_item.question: Why does a wildland fire typically spread much faster up a steep slope than across flat ground?
options: A. Atmospheric oxygen is denser near mountain ridges than in valley bottoms
B. Rising convective heat and closer flame angles preheat and dry the fuels upslope
C. Uphill tree roots pump flammable turpentine to the surface when warmed
D. Gravity pulls smoke downward, leaving clear air above the flame front
choices: A. Atmospheric oxygen is denser near mountain ridges than in valley bottoms
B. Rising convective heat and closer flame angles preheat and dry the fuels upslope
C. Uphill tree roots pump flammable turpentine to the surface when warmed
D. Gravity pulls smoke downward, leaving clear air above the flame front
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Rising convective heat and closer flame angles preheat and dry the fuels upslope
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): On a slope, flames tilt closer to the unburned vegetation above them, and rising hot air preheats and dehydrates upslope fuels so they ignite rapidly (p. 6).

requirements.lead_text: Taking Action. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Taking Action. Do ONE of the following: (a) Develop a fire readiness plan for a wildland area with which you are familiar. The plan should include a map showing available resources, water supplies, natural and manmade barriers, and access. The plan should discuss fuel loads, available fire apparatus, structure protection needs, values at risk, medical and evacuation considerations, and potential fire suppression tactics. (b) Visit with a state or federal forestry official or your local fire warden. Discuss the causes of and types of wildland fire that occur in your area. Discuss the prime fire season(s) in your area. Identify the agency responsible for wildland fire suppression in your area. Discuss what you learned with your counselor. (c) Conduct a Firewise assessment of a home or a building in the wildland-urban interface, which could include a Scout camp building or facility. Identify potential risks and fire hazards. With your counselor's approval, complete a project to reduce the wildfire risk and increase the preparedness of the building. Write a brief report about what you did and learned from the assessment and project. (d) Meet with a Fire Prevention Specialist or a local fire official to learn about fire prevention efforts in your community. From what you learned, prepare a fire prevention message (skit, video, or billboard concept) and share with your counselor and troop (or other group approved by your counselor). (e) Meet with a meteorologist or someone familiar with fire weather and discuss the fire weather concerns and typical fire seasons that exist in your area. Discuss the conditions that lead to a Fire Weather Watch or a Red Flag Warning. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why do severe wildfires frequently lead to destructive flash floods and mudslides when rain falls months after the fire is out?
options: A. Chemical fire retardants turn clay soils into impermeable concrete crusts
B. Surviving trees release excess groundwater through their damaged bark
C. Intense heat destroys root systems and creates hydrophobic soil layers that repel water
D. Ash deposits freeze the upper soil horizon and block snowmelt infiltration
choices: A. Chemical fire retardants turn clay soils into impermeable concrete crusts
B. Surviving trees release excess groundwater through their damaged bark
C. Intense heat destroys root systems and creates hydrophobic soil layers that repel water
D. Ash deposits freeze the upper soil horizon and block snowmelt infiltration
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Intense heat destroys root systems and creates hydrophobic soil layers that repel water
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): High-severity fires vaporize organic compounds that condense into a waxy, water-repellent soil layer while removing the plants and roots that normally absorb rainfall (p. 6).

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Prescribed fire heat melts the waxy resin sealing serotinous cones while clearing surface litter so seeds fall directly onto nutrient-rich mineral soil (p. 9).

B. Rising convective heat and closer flame angles preheat and dry the fuels upslope
C. Uphill tree roots pump flammable turpentine to the surface when warmed
D. Gravity pulls smoke downward, leaving clear air above the flame front
choices: A. Atmospheric oxygen is denser near mountain ridges than in valley bottoms
B. Rising convective heat and closer flame angles preheat and dry the fuels upslope

D. Gravity pulls smoke downward, leaving clear air above the flame front
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Rising convective heat and closer flame angles preheat and dry the fuels upslope
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): On a slope, flames tilt closer to the unburned vegetation above them, and rising hot air preheats and dehydrates upslope fuels so they ignite rapidly (p. 6).
